doc_summary: Buck explains that building settings for high-stakes control research is hard because they need non-saturated, verifiable main tasks plus objectively checkable side tasks that fit the agent's natural affordances. He argues that artificial setups (e.g. side tasks varying arbitrarily per main task) and current real deployments both fall short of representing future risky situations.

items.claim: In a setup, make the side task use affordances the agent legitimately needs for its main tasks instead of an affordance otherwise unused, because any unusual affordance use becomes an easy tell that the blue team (or a monitor/target) can flag.
items.quote: It's sad if the side task requires an affordance that the agent doesn't actually need for its tasks, because the blue team is incentivized to flag any use of that affordance.

items.claim: Distrusts setups where the attack policy is magically told a per-trajectory side task that is arbitrarily paired with the main task, because this is fundamentally unrealistic and prevents studying protocols that give models small context-poor subtasks.
items.quote: The attack policy is magically informed of the side task for each trajectory, but the protocol isn’t. This is fundamentally unrealistic.

items.claim: Prefers objective, checkable definitions of unacceptable behavior over fuzzy ones like 'inserts a security vulnerability' because adversarial optimization will exploit the loosest reading of the definition.
items.quote: if you tried to use a definition like "inserts a security vulnerability", the red team is strongly incentivized to look for the weakest security vulnerabilities that possibly count. (In Ctrl-Z and the original paper, we avoided this by having objective definitions for side task success.)

items.claim: Prefers having the AI generate its own attack ideas over researcher-supplied attacks because it is closer to a capability evaluation of the model and reduces overfitting.
items.quote: It's much nicer to do research if the AI is coming up with the ideas for the attacks itself, rather than just using attacks suggested by the researchers. This is better because it is closer to doing a capability evaluation of the untrusted model and also because it reduces overfitting problems.

items.claim: Distrusts results from iterating against a fixed side-task definition since researchers may leak information about it, making improvements look like genuinely better methods.
items.quote: it's hard to know whether your blue-team strategies are performing better because they're actually better or because you've slowly been leaking bits about the side task definition by iterating against it.

items.claim: Does not think current real AI deployments are good test beds, because agents lack autonomy and access to dangerous resources, so trajectories share little with the future situations of concern.
items.quote: Realistically, AIs right now are not given very much autonomy (mostly because they can't use it productively) or very much access to dangerous resources. So current deployments don't provide us with example trajectories that have that much in common with the situations I'm worried about later.

items.claim: Prefers settings in software engineering and AI-lab-researcher-like computer use over arbitrary domains because the central concern is AIs misusing compute and proprietary models during ML R&D.
items.quote: Because my main concern is AIs misusing their access to compute and proprietary models while doing ML R&D, I'm most interested in settings where the AIs are doing software engineering or using computers for tasks similar to those done by researchers in AI companies.

items.claim: Prefers main tasks that frontier models can do but weaker trusted models do much worse on, over saturated tasks, because otherwise a trusted-model-only protocol trivially wins and the setting is unrepresentative of risky future deployments.
items.quote: We need weaker models to do much worse on these tasks because we want to rule out protocols that just use the trusted model; we think this is more representative of particularly risky deployments in the future.

items.claim: Requires robust measures of main-task success when protocols affect task completion, since the metric gets optimized against during development.
items.quote: We need a robust measure of task success because we optimize against that metric while developing protocols.

items.claim: Regrets underinvesting in setting construction early; setting difficulty is a major, underestimated part of control research cost.
items.quote: When we were writing the first paper in the APPS setting, I did not appreciate how much harder it would be to construct settings for subsequent projects. And I really messed up by not putting more emphasis on this at the start of the Ctrl-Z project.
